_comment: Guided tour for photon-by-photon (Gopich-Szabo) kinetics. It walks the built-in SIMULATOR first -- a molecule whose rates are known -- because the honest question for this method is 'what can my photon budget resolve', and only a known answer settles it. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What this fits
steps.text:
The arrival time and colour of every photon, with no binning at all. That is the whole idea: a bin size is a choice that hides exchange faster than itself, and this method never makes one — it resolves down to the mean interphoton time.

Nine steps. We will start on simulated photons whose rates are known, because the real question here is what your photon budget can resolve.

steps.title: Start where the answer is known
steps.text:
A burst-wise FRET histogram shows a fast-switching molecule as one broadened peak. It cannot say how fast. This method can — but whether it can on your data depends on photon numbers, and no amount of staring at a fit will tell you that.

So switch on the simulator: photons generated from a molecule with rates you set yourself.

steps.title: Set the truth you are going to try to recover
steps.text: Forward and backward rates, and the FRET efficiency of each state. Note the relaxation time they imply — for two states it is 1/(k₁₂ + k₂₁), and that, not either rate alone, is what a measurement actually constrains.

steps.title: The photon budget is the experiment
steps.text:
Photons per burst and number of bursts decide everything about whether the rates come back. Two limits you cannot argue with:

Too fast — exchange quicker than the interphoton time is invisible. At 50 kHz detected, that is about 20 µs.
Too slow — exchange slower than a burst leaves no transition inside a burst to see, and a static mixture will fit better.

Set these to what your real measurement gives you.

steps.title: The tick that rescales every rate
steps.text:
The macro-time resolution converts clock ticks into seconds. Zero reads it from the file header.

Every fitted rate is directly proportional to it, so a wrong value rescales the entire answer — with no other symptom. Nothing in the fit report looks wrong. It is the single most dangerous field in this window on real data.

steps.title: How many states
steps.text: Start at two. An extra state always fits a little better, because it always has more parameters — which is why the number to watch is the BIC, not the likelihood.

steps.title: Fit it
steps.text: The evidence being used is the pattern of colours in time, not their sum. That is what a histogram throws away and why this can see a transition a histogram can only blur.

steps.title: Did you get your rates back?
steps.text:
Compare the fitted rates with what you typed in. This is the step that has no equivalent on real data, and it is the reason to run the simulator first.

Read 1/k rather than k — a waiting time compares directly against the burst duration. If 1/k is much longer than a burst, most bursts contain no transition at all and the rate is poorly determined however confident the fit looks.

steps.title: Then bring your own photons
steps.text:
Untick Simulate, drop the .bur burst tables here, point the folder at the raw files and check the donor/acceptor channel lists.

Two checks before believing the result: does the BIC clearly fall when you add a state (if not, do not add it), and does the H2MM cross-check agree? H2MM fits the same photons in discrete time and shares no likelihood with this — agreement is real evidence.

The ? button has the long version.
